subtopic_detail: sequencing refractive correction before occlusion therapy in unilateral reduced vision found at screening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old boy referred after a preschool vision screening visit. His parents had noticed nothing wrong and say he plays and draws normally.

He was born at term with no perinatal problems and there is no family history of childhood eye disease. On testing, the vision in his right eye is 6/6 and in his left eye is 6/24. The cover test reveals an inward shift of the left eye when the right eye is covered. The red reflex is present, symmetrical and normal in both eyes, and the fundus appears normal on both sides. Cycloplegic refraction has been performed in the clinic.

data_table.Examination: Visual acuity 6/6 right and 6/24 left, cover test shows an inward shift of the left eye on covering the right, red reflex symmetrical and normal bilaterally, fundi normal, ocular movements full
data_table.Investigations: Cycloplegic refraction plus 5.00 dioptres in the left eye and plus 0.75 dioptres in the right eye

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe spectacles for the refractive error and review in four months
options.rationale: Correcting a large difference in refractive power between the eyes is the necessary first treatment, because a substantial proportion of children recover normal vision on spectacles alone over a period of refractive adaptation lasting about three to four months. Occlusion is added only for the deficit that remains after that. (Source: RCH CPG: Vision Screening)

options.text: Commence occlusion of the right eye for six hours daily from today
options.rationale: Patching the better eye before the blurred image is corrected asks the weaker eye to work through an uncorrected 5 dioptre error, which limits what occlusion can achieve and imposes an unnecessary burden on the child. It is the correct second step once spectacles have been worn and the deficit reassessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Vision Screening)

options.text: Refer for surgical correction of the eye alignment within three months
options.rationale: Surgery addresses the cosmetic and sensory consequences of misalignment but does not itself restore vision in the affected eye. In this pattern the deviation is often driven by the uncorrected hypermetropia and improves substantially with spectacles alone. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

options.text: Commence daily atropine drops to the right eye as penalisation therapy
options.rationale: Pharmacological penalisation blurs the better eye and is a recognised alternative to patching with comparable outcomes, particularly where compliance with a patch is poor. Like patching, it belongs after refractive correction rather than before it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

options.text: Repeat the vision screening in twelve months at the school entry check
options.rationale: Visual development is plastic only through the first several years and treatment response falls progressively with age. Deferring for a year in a four year old spends a substantial part of the remaining treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG: Vision Screening)

explanation.summary: Amblyopia is reduced vision in an eye that is structurally normal, caused by the developing visual cortex suppressing a degraded or misaligned image during the sensitive period of visual development. The three mechanisms are a difference in refractive power between the eyes, misalignment, and deprivation from an obstruction such as a cataract or a ptosis, and the first two frequently coexist as they do here. It is the leading cause of monocular vision loss in Australian children and is usually asymptomatic, which is the rationale for preschool screening, since a child with one good eye reports nothing wrong. The normal symmetrical red reflex and normal fundus are important because they exclude deprivational causes including cataract and retinoblastoma, either of which would demand urgent rather than routine referral. Treatment begins with spectacles, worn for a period of refractive adaptation, before occlusion or atropine penalisation is added for residual deficit, and outcomes deteriorate steadily as treatment is started later in childhood.
key_points: Amblyopia is reduced vision in a structurally normal eye and is usually asymptomatic
A normal symmetrical red reflex excludes cataract and retinoblastoma as the cause
Correct the refractive error first and allow three to four months of adaptation
Add occlusion or atropine penalisation only for the residual deficit
Treatment response declines steadily with increasing age at presentation
explanation.pearls: Roughly a third of children with anisometropic amblyopia reach normal acuity on spectacles alone within about sixteen weeks of refractive adaptation, so patching started on the day of diagnosis subjects many children to occlusion they never needed.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

subtopic_detail: identifying the treatable association behind stereotyped cyanotic episodes provoked by crying in a toddler
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing an 18 month old girl whose parents describe three frightening episodes over the past two months. The most recent happened yesterday when she was told she could not have a biscuit before dinner.

She cried hard, then went silent with her mouth open, her lips turned dusky blue and she went floppy and slid to the floor. She was unresponsive for about twenty seconds with a few jerks of her arms at the end, then cried, wanted a cuddle and was back to her usual self within a minute. Each of the three episodes has begun in exactly this way after she was upset or hurt. She is otherwise well, walks and runs normally and has around six bottles of cow's milk a day in addition to her meals.

data_table.Examination: Alert and playful, no murmur, normal heart sounds, femoral pulses palpable and symmetrical, neurological examination normal, development age appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (105 to 135), mean cell volume 68 fL (70 to 86), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (15 to 150), electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with a normal corrected QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange electroencephalography and refer to a paediatric neurologist
options.rationale: Brief jerking at the end of an episode reflects cerebral hypoperfusion rather than a primary seizure, and the constant provoking trigger of crying, the rapid complete recovery and the absence of any drowsy phase afterwards all argue against epilepsy. Investigation is reserved for episodes that occur without a trigger or that are followed by prolonged confusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells)

options.text: Commence oral iron with dietary advice and parental reassurance
options.rationale: These episodes are benign, stereotyped and reliably provoked by crying after an upset, and iron deficiency is a well established association that is present here on the blood film indices and ferritin. Correcting the deficiency reduces both the frequency and the severity of episodes, and excessive cow's milk intake is the usual dietary driver to address alongside it. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells)

options.text: Commence regular sodium valproate and review in the clinic in a month
options.rationale: Anticonvulsant therapy treats a condition she does not have and exposes a toddler to hepatotoxicity and other adverse effects for no benefit. These episodes do not respond to anticonvulsants. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer to paediatric cardiology for a 24 hour Holter monitor recording
options.rationale: Cardiac assessment is warranted when episodes occur during exertion, during swimming, without any provoking trigger, or where there is a family history of premature sudden death. Her electrocardiogram, cardiac examination and femoral pulses are all normal and every episode has followed an emotional trigger. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Advise the parents to avoid confrontation that triggers the episodes
options.rationale: Parents commonly begin to give in to avoid provoking an episode, and warning against this is an important part of counselling, so the advice is exactly backwards. Abandoning normal limit setting reinforces the behaviour without altering the underlying physiology. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells)

explanation.summary: Breath holding spells affect around one in twenty young children, typically begin between six and eighteen months and resolve by about five years of age. The cyanotic form follows a period of vigorous crying after pain, frustration or fright, with expiratory apnoea, colour change, loss of tone and brief loss of consciousness, while the less common pallid form follows a minor bump or fright and is mediated by a vagally driven asystolic pause. Brief tonic stiffening or a few clonic jerks occur in a substantial minority because of transient cerebral hypoperfusion and are frequently misread as a seizure, so the discriminating features are the invariable emotional or painful trigger, the crying that precedes the event, and rapid complete recovery without a postictal phase. Iron deficiency is associated with more frequent and more severe spells, and randomised evidence shows that iron supplementation reduces their frequency, which makes a full blood count and ferritin part of the standard assessment. Excessive cow's milk intake beyond about 500 mL a day in a toddler is the commonest dietary cause of the deficiency, and parents need explicit advice to maintain normal boundaries rather than avoid triggers.
key_points: Episodes are always preceded by crying after an upset, pain or fright
Brief jerking reflects cerebral hypoperfusion, not epilepsy
Check a full blood count and ferritin because iron deficiency worsens spells
Iron supplementation reduces both frequency and severity
Counsel parents to keep normal limits rather than avoid triggers
explanation.pearls: Cow's milk intake above about 500 mL a day in a toddler displaces iron rich foods and causes occult gut blood loss, and reducing it while giving three months of oral iron is what actually reduces breath holding spell frequency.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: recognising that raised transaminases with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase are of muscle origin
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old boy referred by a gastroenterology colleague for a second opinion. He was referred to that clinic three months ago after routine bloods taken during an episode of gastroenteritis showed raised liver enzymes, and repeat testing has shown the same pattern.

His parents mention that he is slower than the other children at kindergarten, falls frequently, and climbs the stairs at home one step at a time putting the same foot first. He walked at 19 months and his speech is also behind his peers. When you ask him to get up from sitting on the floor he turns onto his front and pushes on his own thighs with his hands to stand. His calves look bulky for his build.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral calf hypertrophy, proximal lower limb weakness, positive Gowers manoeuvre, waddling gait, reflexes present at the knees, no hepatomegaly and no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L (less than 35), gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits, bilirubin within normal limits, albumin within normal limits, creatine kinase 12400 U/L (less than 200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Open muscle biopsy of the quadriceps with immunohistochemical staining
options.rationale: Biopsy with dystrophin staining was formerly the standard confirmatory test and retains a role when genetic testing is negative despite a strong clinical picture. Performing it first subjects the child to a general anaesthetic for information that a blood test usually provides. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

options.text: Liver ultrasound with viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen
options.rationale: This pursues the referral that has already been made in error. A gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits alongside raised transaminases indicates that the enzymes are coming from skeletal muscle rather than from liver, since hepatocellular injury characteristically raises the gamma glutamyl transferase as well. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

options.text: Dystrophin gene testing for deletions and duplications on a blood sample
options.rationale: Progressive proximal weakness with calf hypertrophy, a positive Gowers manoeuvre and a creatine kinase in the thousands is a dystrophinopathy until proven otherwise, and genetic testing on blood confirms the diagnosis in around seven in ten boys through deletion or duplication analysis. It avoids an operation and immediately informs carrier testing and reproductive counselling for the family. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

options.text: Electromyography with nerve conduction studies under sedation
options.rationale: Electrophysiology can demonstrate a myopathic pattern but cannot identify which myopathy, so it does not reach a diagnosis. It has largely been displaced by genetic testing in this situation and is poorly tolerated by young children. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Repeat liver function tests and creatine kinase in three months
options.rationale: A further three months of observation delays a diagnosis that carries immediate implications for corticosteroid timing, cardiac and respiratory surveillance and genetic counselling for the family. The abnormality has already been confirmed on repeat testing. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy affects roughly one in 3500 to 5000 boys and follows X linked recessive inheritance, with about a third of cases arising from new mutations so that a negative family history is common. Presentation is typically between two and five years with delayed walking, frequent falls, difficulty with stairs and running, and a positive Gowers manoeuvre, and around a third of boys also have global developmental delay or language delay because dystrophin is expressed in brain as well as muscle. A recurring diagnostic detour is referral for liver disease, because damaged muscle releases alanine and aspartate aminotransferase and these are reported on standard liver panels, so a normal gamma glutamyl transferase alongside raised transaminases in a boy with motor difficulty should redirect thinking to muscle and prompt a creatine kinase. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroid therapy started at the appropriate stage prolongs ambulation, and structured cardiac and respiratory surveillance changes long term outcome. Genetic confirmation also enables carrier testing of female relatives and access to mutation specific therapies.
key_points: Transaminases rise from damaged skeletal muscle and appear on standard liver panels
A normal gamma glutamyl transferase points away from a hepatic source
Creatine kinase in the thousands with a positive Gowers manoeuvre is the key combination
About a third of boys have associated developmental or language delay
Genetic testing on blood confirms most cases and avoids muscle biopsy
explanation.pearls: In any boy under five referred for unexplained raised transaminases, check the gamma glutamyl transferase and a creatine kinase before imaging the liver; a normal gamma glutamyl transferase with a creatine kinase above 2000 U/L redirects the entire workup to muscle.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists
